n01: Lawyers don't need an agent that sounds confident. They need one that can prove what it says, or admit what it can't. This is Traceable Counsel. Five agents, one shared Meko datapack, one fictional WeChat case. Every conclusion cites its evidence, or says it cannot be verified. The case: a fictional delivery dispute. Two hundred gift boxes, forty-eight thousand, twenty thousand paid, balance disputed.
n02: The Screener admitted two messages: an order and an acceptance. That's the contract.
n03: The Event Extractor turns those two messages into one event, once. It is now shared memory.
n04: The Strategy Agent needs the contract. It reads the event, not the chat. One search, no re-read.
n05: The reviewer attacks the same claim, from the same shared event. If the event were wrong, both agents would be wrong together, and we would see it in one place.
n06: One agent's learning becomes every agent's advantage, and the audit trail shows it.
n07: The chain for this event is complete. The next event is not, and that matters in scene B.
n08: Now the test that matters. I am asking for a conclusion the evidence does not support.
n09: The draft almost upgrades a promise into an admission. The reviewer catches it.
n10: Here is the whole answer, in under two minutes. No written admission exists in this case. The closest item is a promise, and a promise is not an admission.
n11: So the system downgrades the claim to what the evidence actually says, and hands the legal judgment back to a human.
n12: And it tells you what would change its mind: a written admission, and photos of the alleged damage. That list is generated, not hand-written.
n13: Show your work, or say you can't. That's the whole system.
